name: Pas-ta'ai (Short Spirit Ceremony)
description: After nightfall, a bright chiming rises through the valley — the "hip bells" (tapa:ngasan), hung with tiny brass bells, ringing all night long in time with the dancers' steps. This is the Saisiyat Pas-ta'ai, the Ceremony of the Short People (also known as Pasta'ai), a ceremony bound by strict ritual rules. It is not held to ask for blessings. It is held to console the spirits of the legendary Short People (Ta'ai), who taught the Saisiyat how to farm but were killed through a plot laid by the tribe, leaving a curse behind as they died. To calm the spirits' anger and pray for the community's safety, the Saisiyat hold a minor ceremony every two years and a grand ceremony every ten, each lasting four days and three nights. The singing and dancing run from sunset to sunrise, solemn and hushed, full of awe and remorse toward the spirits of the Short People.
story: Legend says that long ago the Saisiyat and the short-statured Ta'ai lived as neighbors on opposite banks of a river. The Ta'ai were skilled in farming and in magic, and they taught the Saisiyat how to cultivate the land; for a time the two peoples were close. But according to the legend, the Ta'ai repeatedly offended Saisiyat women, until the tribe could bear it no longer. They set a trap and drowned nearly all of the Ta'ai in the river. Only two survived. The survivors did not strike back. Instead they left a curse — the Saisiyat would face failed harvests and misfortune — and at the same time they taught them, line by line, the songs, dances, and rules of a ceremony to be held year after year in search of forgiveness. Then they turned and walked away. Ever since, the Saisiyat have held the Pas-ta'ai, generation after generation. There is no winner in this story. What it remembers is a kindness, a wrong, and the remorse a people still carry through a whole night of song and dance.
worship: The Pas-ta'ai is nothing like an ordinary prayer-for-blessings festival — there is no incense and no statue. Its heart is atonement and reconciliation, and the people speak to the spirits of the Short People directly, through song, dance, and ritual. The ceremony runs roughly like this: setting the date beforehand, welcoming the spirits, entertaining the spirits, and finally driving off and sending away the spirits; smearing mud, grabbing silver grass, and similar acts all take place during the send-off at dawn on the last day. Quarreling is forbidden while the ceremony lasts, and people tie on silver grass to ward off evil. Each clan has its own role: the Zhu clan leads the rites, the Ri clan shoots the opening arrow, and the ceremonial flag is carried by one young man from each of the three major clans. There are fifteen ceremonial songs, each with a fixed order and meaning, sung through the whole night.
festivals: The Pas-ta'ai is held in the middle of the tenth lunar month (roughly November to December), at two ritual grounds that each set their own dates: the Southern Group at Xiangtianhu in Nanzhuang Township, Miaoli County, and the Northern Group at Daai in Wufeng Township, Hsinchu County. The ceremony lasts four days and three nights; for the grand ceremony held once every ten years, an additional ceremonial flag (sinaton) is made. The first night is the "Welcoming of the Spirits": the whole community lines up at the ritual ground as the lead elder chants the welcoming song. The second and third nights are the "Entertaining of the Spirits": the people form a great circle and keep singing and dancing until daybreak, the hip bells and voices echoing through the valley — a sight both grand and solemn. Dawn on the last day brings the "Sending Off of the Spirits," the saddest moment of all, as the people sing the farewell songs and watch the spirits of the Short People depart. The Pas-ta'ai was designated a National Important Folk Custom in 2013. Outsiders may attend, but please check the visiting guidelines with the community or organizers beforehand, and respect the awe the Saisiyat hold toward the spirits of the Short People.

temples.name: Xiangtianhu Ritual Ground
temples.deityStory: Home of the Southern Group's Pas-ta'ai, and one of the ceremony's main sites.

temples.name: Wufeng Ritual Ground
temples.deityStory: Home of the Northern Group's Pas-ta'ai.

name: Alizu (Ancestral Spirit)
domain: Siraya ancestral spirit, guardian of the community, rain prayers, healing
description: Step into a Siraya kuwa, the community ritual house, and you will find no statue at all — only a pot wrapped in red cloth, quietly holding water. This is Alizu (also called Ali-Mu or Taizu). Alizu is the most revered ancestral spirit of the Siraya, one of Taiwan's plains Indigenous peoples. Unlike the sculpted deities of Han Chinese temples, Alizu has no fixed form; the spirit's power is represented by pots, bottles, and jars filled with water, a practice known as "pot worship." The pot is bound in red cloth, and the water inside, called "Xiang water," is believed to heal, drive off evil, and bring blessings. The kuwa is not only the center of the faith but also where the community meets to deliberate. Each village's "Night Ceremony" is its most important rite, and every village holds it on its own date: people offer betel nut and rice wine and, hand in hand, circle and sing the ancient qian qu songs in gratitude for the ancestors' protection.
story: Alizu is not one particular deity but the Siraya people's collective name for their ancestral spirits — spirits who watch over the community's births, aging, sickness, and death, and who also move the workings of nature. Dutch rule and the wave of sinicization under the Qing dealt heavy blows to Siraya tradition; language, surnames, and ways of life were changed bit by bit. Yet pot worship held on stubbornly and became the clearest marker of Siraya identity. One of the best-known beliefs handed down through the generations is "Xiang water healing": the pot water blessed by Alizu is believed to cure every illness. In the kuwa, the "General Pillar" stands for Alizu's authority and power. Today, Danei, Jiali, Dongshan, and other places in Tainan still keep complete kuwa and Night Ceremony traditions, so the life of this Austronesian ancestral faith carries on in the qian qu songs sung through the night.

temples.name: Tainan Danei Toushe Kuwa
temples.deityStory: Toushe is the most distinctive representative of the Mugaliuwan community, and holds its Night Ceremony every year on the 14th–15th days of the tenth lunar month.

temples.name: Jiali Beitouyang Lichang Temple
temples.deityStory: Beitouyang is the former home of the Soulangh community of the Siraya. Lichang Temple enshrines Alizu and preserves the traditional pot worship and Xiang water rites. Its main Night Ceremony falls on the 28th–29th days of the third lunar month.

associatedTemples: Tainan Danei Toushe Kuwa (Danei District, Tainan City)
Jiali Beitouyang Lichang Temple (Jiali District, Tainan City)
worship: Alizu is honored in a way entirely different from Han Chinese temples, keeping the original ritual character of the Austronesian peoples: the place of worship is the kuwa rather than a temple, and the sacred symbol is a water-filled pot rather than a statue. Worshippers offer betel nut, rice wine, and tobacco, and the rites are led by the "ang-i," the female priestesses. The ang-i hold great standing among the Siraya — they can communicate with the ancestral spirits, heal the sick, and divine good and ill fortune. At the core of the ritual is the Xiang water, the pot water blessed by Alizu, believed to heal and ward off evil; and in matters large and small, people also come to the kuwa to ask Alizu for guidance. The rites are led jointly by elders and the ang-i.
festivals: The most important Siraya rite is the "Night Ceremony," and each village holds it on a different date: Toushe in Danei on the 14th–15th days of the tenth lunar month, Jibeishua in Dongshan on the 5th day of the ninth lunar month, and Beitouyang in Jiali on the 28th–29th days of the third lunar month. The ceremony begins at night and lasts until dawn. The ang-i lead the people in singing the qian qu; dressed in white, everyone joins hands in a great circle and welcomes the ancestral spirits with ancient melodies. Pigs are also offered during the ceremony. The "Siraya Night Ceremony of Jibeishua, Dongshan" was registered as a National Important Folk Custom in 2013. In recent years the Siraya have worked hard to revive their culture, and the Night Ceremony has become an important window onto Taiwan's plains Indigenous cultures.

name: Paiwan Hundred Pacer Snake Belief
domain: Guardian of chiefly families, protector of the community, symbol of nobility and courage
description: On the lintels of Paiwan slate houses, on wood carvings, clay pots, and festival clothing, the same figure appears again and again — the coiled hundred-pacer viper. In Paiwan and Rukai culture the hundred-pacer holds the highest place of honor, seen as an embodiment of the ancestors and a guardian spirit. The Paiwan believe their ancestors share an inseparable blood bond with the hundred-pacer: it is the guardian of chiefly families and the spiritual symbol of the whole community. That is why hundred-pacer motifs cover clothing, carvings, buildings, and everyday objects, making it the core symbol of Paiwan culture — not just a pattern, but a whole people's memory of where they came from.
story: In the Paiwan creation legend, the sun laid eggs on the sacred mountain of Dawu, placed them in a clay pot, and set a hundred-pacer to guard them; from those eggs hatched the ancestors of the Paiwan. So the hundred-pacer is the guardian of the ancestors, bound especially closely to the people. Another legend, shared by the Paiwan and the Rukai, tells of a chief's daughter who married a hundred-pacer that had taken human form, and from them descended the chiefly lineage — which explains why only chiefly families have the right to use the hundred-pacer motif. In the strict Paiwan class system, the hundred-pacer motif marks noble status, and commoners may not use it freely.

temples.name: Mount Kavulungan (Sacred Mountain)
temples.deityStory: Mount Dawu (Kavulungan) is the sacred mountain of the Paiwan and Rukai, regarded as the dwelling place of the ancestral spirits. The people believe that after death the souls of their ancestors return to Dawu to be reunited with the hundred-pacer ancestral spirit. Dawu is also the direction many important ceremonies face in reverence.

worship: For the Paiwan, the hundred-pacer pattern is not decoration anyone can use: it belongs to the chiefly class, a symbol of status and lineage, and commoners may not use it freely. That is why the hundred-pacer always appears in the most important places — carrying a family's memory, and carrying the protection of the ancestral spirits.
festivals: The Five-Year Ceremony (Maljeveq, also called the Covenant Between Humans and Spirits) is held once every five years, and only in some communities, such as Gulou in Laiyi Township, Lili in Chunri Township, and Tuban in Daren Township. At its heart is welcoming the ancestral spirits back to the community to be reunited with the living. The climax is the "ball-piercing" rite: warriors thrust long bamboo poles at rattan balls tossed into the air, and whoever pierces one is believed to have received the ancestors' blessing.

name: Tayal Ancestral Spirit Belief (Utux)
domain: Protecting the people, upholding social order, guiding morality and ethics
description: For the Atayal, there is an invisible measuring stick for how to live and how to act, and it is called gaga. At the core of Atayal belief are two words: Utux (the ancestral spirits) and gaga (ancestral teachings and norms). Utux are the souls of departed ancestors, who the Atayal believe always watch over their descendants. The will of the ancestors is passed down through gaga — a body of traditional law covering morality, social norms, and ritual taboos that guides people in how to live and how to treat one another. Those who keep gaga receive the ancestors' protection; those who break it are punished. Gaga is not written on paper. It lives in the words and deeds of every Atayal person.
story: Atayal origin legends come in different traditions. One says that at Pinsbkan (around today's Ruiyan, in Ren'ai Township, Nantou) a great rock split open and the first Atayal ancestors stepped out; another tradition names Mount Papak Waqa as the ancestors' place of origin. The first ancestors taught their descendants to hunt, weave, and farm, and set down gaga for the people. The best-known Atayal tradition is facial tattooing (patas): a man had to prove his courage in headhunting and a woman had to master weaving before earning the right to the tattoo that marked adulthood and honor. But the tattoo's meaning reached beyond this world. The Atayal believe that after death the soul walks toward the "Rainbow Bridge" (Hongu Utux), and on its far side lies the land of the ancestors. The ancestral spirits guard the bridge, and only souls who kept gaga all their lives and earned the right to the facial tattoo may cross it and meet their ancestors again. The lines on a person's face became, in this way, a passage home to the ancestors.

temples.name: Mount Papak Waqa (Sacred Mountain)
temples.deityStory: Mount Dabajian (Papak Waqa) is the sacred mountain of the Atayal, regarded as the birthplace of the people. In one Atayal origin tradition, this is where the ancestors came from, which gives the mountain its sacred standing; facing it, the people offer prayers as a sign of respect.

associatedTemples: Mount Papak Waqa (Jianshi Township, Hsinchu County / Tai'an Township, Miaoli County)
worship: Atayal worship centers on prayer to the ancestral spirits. There are no fixed temples; rites take place in the community's gathering house or out in the mountains and forests. Millet wine is essential, along with meat — pork, or game such as muntjac. An elder leads the people in praying to the ancestors, reporting the community's affairs, large and small, to Utux and asking for guidance and protection. It is less a petition to a deity than descendants quietly talking with the ancestors who have always been watching over them.
festivals: The most important Atayal ceremony is the Ancestral Spirit Ceremony (Ma'aho, also called Smyus), held after the millet harvest, with each community choosing its own date. The whole community gathers, and elders lead them in offering newly harvested millet and millet wine to the ancestral spirits, giving thanks for a year of protection and renewing the bond with those who came before.

name: Bunun Sky God Belief (Dihanin)
domain: Ruler of heaven, earth, and all things; giver of good harvests; protector of the sun-shooting hero
description: When the Bunun look up at the moon, they see more than its waxing and waning — they see when to sow, when to weed, when to harvest, and which ceremony comes next. Bunun belief holds Dihanin (the Sky God, or Heaven) as the highest spiritual power, ruling over everything between heaven and earth: the weather, the growth of crops, even human fate. Among Taiwan's Indigenous peoples, the Bunun place the greatest weight on the calendar and on farming rituals. Following the phases of the moon, they developed a precise agricultural calendar in which every month has its own rites and taboos, linked one to the next into a complete system of belief built around growing millet. The Sky God is not far away; Dihanin is there in every full moon and every row of millet.
story: The most famous Bunun legend is the story of shooting the sun. In ancient times two suns took turns blazing in the sky. The heat dried up the rivers and scorched the crops, and the people suffered terribly. A warrior of the community resolved to shoot one of the suns down, and set out with his young son toward the place where the sun rises. Father and son crossed mountain after mountain and walked for a very long time — so long that the orange tree the father had planted on his way out had grown tall. At last they reached the edge of the sky. The warrior drew his bow and struck one of the suns with a single arrow. The wounded sun slowly dimmed and became the moon we see today. The moon seized the warrior, and after he repented, the moon taught him the ways of worship and its taboos — which is why the Bunun hold their ceremonies by the moon. From then on there was one sun and one moon in the sky, and life returned to the land.

temples.name: Jade Mountain (Sacred Mountain)
temples.location: Nantou County / Chiayi County / Kaohsiung City
temples.deityStory: Jade Mountain is the heart of the Bunun traditional territory, regarded as the place closest to the Sky God Dihanin. Important Bunun ceremonies are performed facing Jade Mountain, asking the Sky God for protection.

associatedTemples: Jade Mountain (Nantou County / Chiayi County / Kaohsiung City)
worship: Bunun offerings are mainly millet wine and meat, and an elder or priest leads the people in praying to Dihanin. The Bunun also have a unique "pictographic calendar," which records the farm work and ceremonies of each month in picture symbols; the scholar Mabuchi Toichi considered it a priest's memo for keeping track of ritual matters. The most unforgettable part of their worship is the eight-part polyphonic chant (Pasibutbut): the people stand in a circle and, with harmonies stacked layer upon layer, sing a prayer for a good millet harvest. It is not a performance. It is a whole community lifting its wishes to the Sky God together, in one voice made of many.
festivals: The most important Bunun ceremony is the Ear-Shooting Festival (Malahtangia), held every year around April and May. It is a hunting festival: boys take part in the ear shooting, praying to grow into good hunters, and the songs chanted are the boasting of feats (malastapang). The internationally known eight-part polyphony (Pasibutbut, also called the Prayer for a Millet Harvest) is sung during the season when millet is sown and growing (roughly January to March), asking the Sky God for a good millet harvest; it was registered as a National Important Traditional Performing Art in 2010. The Japanese musicologist Kurosawa Takatomo recorded the song in 1943 and sent it to the international folk music community in 1952, drawing attention from around the world.

name: Tao Ocean Spirit Belief (Anito)
domain: Protection at sea, the gift of flying fish, driving away evil spirits
description: Every spring, schools of flying fish return to the waters off Orchid Island, and the whole rhythm of Tao life for the year starts moving with them. The Tao (also called the Yami) live on Orchid Island (Lanyu), an Indigenous people whose culture is built around the sea. Their belief centers on Anito (souls, spirits) and holds that all things have spirits. Within it, the beliefs and rites around flying fish form the most distinctive chapter of Tao culture: flying fish are seen as a sacred food given by the heavens, and around how they are caught, eaten, and the taboos attached to them, a whole set of strict cultural rules has grown. For the Tao, how they treat these fish is how they keep their covenant with the sea and with their ancestors.
story: The Tao legend of the flying fish begins like this. In ancient times, the people did not yet know how to tell one kind of fish from another, and they cooked flying fish together with other fish — and one after another, people fell ill. One night the God of the Flying Fish, a black-winged flying fish, came to an old man in a dream. It told him that flying fish were a sacred gift from the heavens meant especially for the Tao, and must be cooked in their own pots, never mixed with other fish. The Flying Fish God also taught the old man in detail how to catch flying fish, the rules for eating them, and all their taboos. When the old man woke, he passed these teachings on to his people, and from then on the Tao built a cultural system around the flying fish. When fishing may begin, when it must stop, how the fish are preserved and shared — this whole body of flying fish season rules became the foundation of social order among the Tao.

temples.name: Orchid Island Communities
temples.deityStory: Each of Orchid Island's six communities (Yeyou, Yuren, Hongtou, Langdao, Dongqing, and Yeyin) has its own boathouses and places of worship. The Tao have no fixed temples; rites are held on the shore, in the boathouses, or in the community square.

associatedTemples: Orchid Island community ritual grounds (Lanyu Township, Taitung County)
worship: Tao worship does not happen in temples; it is bound up with the sea and the natural world. Before the flying fish season arrives, the men go down to the shore to hold the "Calling the Fish" ceremony, summoning the flying fish to come. When a new plank boat is launched, there is also a solemn launching ceremony, praying for safe voyages and good catches. These rules are how the people put their reverence for the sea into practice, every time they head out to sea.
festivals: The Tao "Flying Fish Festival" is their central ceremony, held in three stages: the spring "Calling the Fish" ceremony (mivanwa), when the people gather on the shore to summon the flying fish; the summer "Storing" ceremony, when the catch is dried in the sun for keeping; and the autumn "Final Eating" ceremony, when the flying fish season formally ends — dried flying fish that have been hung up may not be thrown away carelessly, but may be fed to pigs and dogs as a sign of respect. The "New Boat Launching Ceremony" is another important rite. The Tao plank boat (tatala) is built by hand from many kinds of wood fitted together, its hull painted with traditional patterns in red, white, and black, and its launching is solemn and sacred.

name: Puyuma Ancestral Spirit Belief (Palakuwan)
domain: Guardian of the community's young men, passing on cultural knowledge, upholding social order
description: In a traditional Puyuma community, a boy first trains in the junior meeting house (takuban), then moves up into the youth meeting house, the Palakuwan, where the young men live and learn together. This is the heart of the traditional belief system of the Puyuma (Pinuyumayan): their ancestral spirit faith. The Palakuwan is more than a building; it is where Puyuma ancestral belief, age-grade organization, and cultural inheritance take concrete form. It differs from Han Chinese folk religion in one fundamental way — there is no ranking of "gods" above "humans" here. The ancestors are not deities set on high but "those who went before," still connected to community life, and their wisdom, norms, and protection continue to reach later generations through the rites of the Palakuwan. The Puyuma live mainly in Beinan Township and Taitung City in Taitung County, and the Nanwang community (Puyuma) places special emphasis on its annual ceremony ('Amiyan), which is large in scale and fully preserved.
story: A Puyuma boy grows up step by step inside the Palakuwan. Traditional Puyuma society has a strict age-grade system: males rise from the boyhood grade (takubakuban) up to the young men's grade (bangsaran), and each grade has its own tasks and responsibilities in the meeting house. Elders in the house pass down, by word of mouth, the ancestors' stories, the community's history, and the skills of daily life, one telling at a time. In Puyuma belief, the ancestral spirits dwell not only in the community but also among the mountains, rivers, and land — the return of game and the abundance of crops are both seen as the ancestors' blessing. This inheritance once came close to breaking. Under Japanese rule, the Kominka assimilation policy suppressed Indigenous traditions, and after the war Protestant and Catholic churches came into the communities and many families converted. Yet the Palakuwan and the annual ceremony, at the core of it all, did not vanish entirely, because the people protected them. After the 1980s, as the Indigenous rights movement rose, young Puyuma also took up the work of carrying on the meeting house and the annual ceremony.

temples.name: Nanwang Community (Puyuma)
temples.deityStory: The Nanwang community places special emphasis on the annual ceremony and still holds the Great Hunting Ceremony and the Monkey Ceremony today, large in scale and fully preserved.

temples.name: Jhihben Community (Katipul)
temples.deityStory: The Jhihben community is the center of the Puyuma legend of ancestors "born from stone" (the "born from bamboo" legend belongs to Nanwang). Jhihben places special emphasis on its Harvest Festival every July.

worship: Puyuma ancestral worship is something quite different from a Han Chinese temple. The traditional Palakuwan is a space for men only, and outsiders — especially women and non-Puyuma — may not enter at will. Worship centers on oral recitation, chanting, prayer, and offerings: elders speak to the ancestral spirits in the Puyuma language, reporting matters, asking for protection, and giving thanks for their care. Offerings are mostly betel nut, rice wine, homemade pottery-jar wine, game, and crops, reflecting a spirit of "sharing daily life with the ancestors." Today some communities open certain areas to outside visitors during the annual ceremony, but that openness comes with conditions: visitors should obtain the community's permission in advance, follow the dress guidelines, not photograph certain rites at will, not pass careless judgment, and accept the guidance of community members. In the end, the first lesson in understanding Puyuma culture is respecting the Puyuma as the rightful owners of their own culture.
festivals:
**Annual Ceremony ('Amiyan)**: Held every year from around December 24 to around January 2 of the following year, this is the most important traditional Puyuma rite. It includes the boys' **Monkey Ceremony (mangamangayaw)** and the men's **Great Hunting Ceremony (mangayaw)**: boys enter the junior meeting house through the Monkey Ceremony, and are promoted to young men only after the Great Hunting Ceremony. The Nanwang community places special emphasis on the annual ceremony, which there is large in scale and fully preserved.

**Harvest Festival**: Held every year in mid-July after the millet is harvested, celebrating the millet harvest. The Jhihben community places special emphasis on the Harvest Festival, while the Harvest Festival at Chulu is known for its swing.

**The meaning of community rites today** — Puyuma ceremonies such as the annual ceremony and the Harvest Festival have moved beyond purely religious meaning to become **a concrete expression of ethnic and cultural identity, a setting for educating young people in their culture, and a window for cultural exchange between peoples**. Every year they draw Puyuma home from the cities to take part, making them important seasons for passing on Taiwan's Indigenous cultures.
